lesson_title: The Turnstile, the Ticket and the Corridor
hook_text: Your circuit is secretly a stadium: a turnstile, a ticket price, and one very crowded corridor.
clip_script: Current is counting at a point: how many supporters click through the turnstile each second. Not how fast anyone walks, not how full the stadium is — clicks per second at the gate. In a circuit the supporters are coulombs, and one coulomb through per second is one ampere. Forty coulombs in eight seconds? Five a second — five amps. And here is the fear this picture dissolves: current never gets eaten along the way. Watch the turnstile — every supporter who enters comes out the other side. The gate swallows nobody. Current is identical on both sides of a bulb. What the bulb collects is the energy each charge carries — the ticket money, never the people. The battery? It is the pump on the roof, loading every coulomb with a parcel of energy before the lap: volts are just joules per coulomb, the size of the parcel. And resistance is the corridor at break time: electrons bumping through a jittery crowd of ions, paying energy at every bump — that is why wires warm up and kettle elements glow. Longer corridor, harder. Narrower, harder. Hotter, harder. Turnstile, ticket, pump, corridor: four pictures, and the whole of circuits belongs to you.
visual_style: A stylised stadium gate with glowing coulomb-supporters clicking through and a counter racing; a rooftop pump loading energy parcels onto each one; a corridor scene where a glowing electron bumps through rattling ions leaving heat trails; scoreboard-style labels for amps and volts.
mood: Match-day energy applied to a first circuit.
pacing: Quick turnstile open with the counter ticking, a beat on nobody-vanishes, brisk pump and corridor scenes, four-picture recap at full speed.
